Who sets and collects the tax

Property tax on a Virginia house is a local matter. Your county, city, or town sends the bill, not the state, and each one decides its own rates, due dates, and relief programs.

Two offices split the job. The commissioner of the revenue values your property and corrects mistakes. The treasurer takes payment and chases delinquent accounts. You will find both on your locality's website. Request a payoff figure from the treasurer when a closing approaches.

How a house is valued for tax

Real estate is taxable unless an exemption applies, and each reassessment targets 100 percent of fair market value (Va. Code 58.1-3201). Your bill rests on what the locality thinks the house would sell for, whatever you paid.

The schedule varies. A county reassesses every four years, or every three when its board of supervisors votes that way. A county with 50,000 people or fewer can stretch to five or six years, and Augusta and Bedford counties may too (Va. Code 58.1-3252). A county or city that employs a qualified full-time appraiser can pass an ordinance for annual or two-year assessment, valuing property as of January 1 (section 3253).

Who assessesHow oftenStatute
County general reassessment4 years, or 3 if supervisors vote58.1-3252
County of 50,000 people or fewerOption of a 5 or 6 year cycle58.1-3252
Locality with a qualified full-time appraiserEvery 2 years or yearly, by local ordinance58.1-3253

Due dates and penalties

The calendar is a local decision. A locality may bill once or in two equal installments, and it fixes penalties and interest by ordinance (section 3916). Two neighboring localities may not share a schedule, so read the treasurer's calendar for your own address.

Localities cannot pile on charges without limit. Interest can start the next day, at no more than 10 percent a year, with a higher cap from the second year of delinquency onward. A late penalty may reach 10 percent of the overdue amount or $10, whichever is more, but not beyond the tax itself. Fees for collection or attorneys can be added if contracted for, at up to 20 percent of the delinquent tax.

The statute also gives some breathing room:

  • For good cause, a locality may extend payment by as much as 90 days.
  • A service member deployed outside the country is automatically extended on the tax for a primary residence until 90 days after deployment ends.
  • When a local official caused the late assessment, there is no penalty if the bill is paid within two weeks of notice.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the assessor, move on to the local board of equalization, and finish at the circuit court if needed. The board assumes the assessor's number is right and can lower or raise it. You win by showing, with the greater weight of the evidence, that the house is valued above fair market value, or that the assessment is uneven and ignored accepted appraisal practice (section 3379).

Comparable sales through the December 31 before the effective date can be used as evidence, if they reach the locality by its deadline. Owners of a home with under four residential units are entitled to written notice from the assessor, and to the assessment records within 15 days of a written request.

Two other routes remain open:

  • The commissioner of the revenue can correct an error if you apply within three years after the tax year ends or one year after assessment, whichever is later. For real estate this means the commissioner's own mistakes or factual errors in a general reassessment (section 3980).
  • The circuit court takes applications within three years after the last day of the tax year, or one year after assessment or the end of an earlier appeal, whichever is later. It starts from the same presumption of correctness (section 3984).

Appeals work best when you bring paper. Gather your last assessment notice, a few recent sales of similar houses near yours, photos of defects that lower value, and any repair estimates. Put them in order before the hearing, and write down the exact figure you think is fair so the board has something specific to decide on.

While an administrative appeal is pending, the bill does not go delinquent, provided you filed within 90 days of the assessment. The pause extends 30 days past the final decision.

Exemptions and deferrals for older owners

Relief of this kind appears only where a locality has voted for it. Under Va. Code 58.1-3210, a county, city, or town may pass an ordinance that exempts or defers tax for owners age 65 and up, or permanently and totally disabled if the ordinance includes that group, as long as the home is their only dwelling.

An ordinance may limit the break to growth in the tax since the owner turned 65 or became disabled. Homes held through a life estate, a revocable trust the owner controls, or certain irrevocable trusts may qualify. A leasehold does not. Income and net worth limits are local, so ask your local assessing office what applies.

Selling with taxes owed

Closing settles the bill. The tax lien sits above all others until the locality is paid, and a purchaser, a foreclosure trustee included, must send proceeds to the taxes and levies on that property (Va. Code 58.1-3340). Penalty and interest are treated as tax here, and current-year rents fall under the lien as well.

The sales contract prorates the seller's share. One timing quirk: a sale after January 1, once bills are out, lets the treasurer withdraw the old owner's bill and send a new one to the buyer, penalty free if paid within two weeks.

When taxes are years behind

A locality can go to court to sell a house over unpaid tax. The usual trigger is taxes still unpaid on December 31 following the second anniversary of the due date. Properties that are condemned, a nuisance, derelict, or designated blighted qualify after one year. A property assessed at $100,000 or less can be sold on a court finding after the first anniversary (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

Before suing, the collecting officer has to send notice to the address on file and to the property at least 30 days in advance, and the list goes into a local newspaper. Paying the full balance before the sale redeems the property, but a partial payment will not end the suit. An installment agreement of up to 72 months can put the sale on hold, so long as current taxes are also kept up.

If the property sells for more than is owed, the former owner and heirs are entitled to the surplus left after taxes, penalties, interest, fees, costs, and liens. Claims must come within two years of confirmation, or the money goes to the locality (Va. Code 58.1-3967).

Taxes and a quick sale

What you owe at closing counts for more than the offer price. Get a fresh tax statement from the treasurer before accepting anything, and have the title company list each lien. Budget for the state recordation tax of 25 cents per $100 and the grantor tax of 50 cents per $500, which falls on the seller unless the contract moves it (Va. Code 58.1-802).

A sensible routine before you sign anything: pull your latest bill, note whether the first half or both halves are paid, and write down the name and phone number of the treasurer's clerk who gave you the figure. Bring the bill to your first conversation with a buyer. When the numbers on paper match what the title company finds, closing day moves faster and fewer surprises come out of your proceeds.

Tell the title company early if you have an open assessment appeal, a local deferral, or an installment plan with the treasurer. Any of them can change the payoff, and a cash buyer can plan around them when they are disclosed up front.

Frequently asked questions

Who handles questions about my bill?

The treasurer collects it, and the commissioner of the revenue or an equivalent office sets the value. Both are local, not state, offices.

How often does my house get reassessed?

Counties must do it every four years, or every three if supervisors vote for it. Small counties may use five or six years, and a locality with a qualified appraiser can assess every year or every other year.

What is the maximum late charge?

The penalty may reach 10 percent of the overdue tax or $10, whichever is greater, but never more than the tax. Interest is limited to 10 percent a year, higher after the first year of delinquency.

Can I list my house during a tax appeal?

Yes. The tax stays a lien, so closing pays it from proceeds. Tell the title company about the appeal so the payoff comes out right.

When can a locality sell a house for unpaid tax?

Usually after delinquency on December 31 past the second anniversary of the due date. One year is enough for condemned, nuisance, derelict, or blighted property, and for property assessed at $100,000 or less with a court finding.

What the homestead exemption protects

Virginia's homestead exemption keeps a householder's property out of reach of creditor process on a debt, up to the dollar limits in Va. Code 34-4. It guards against debt collection. It has nothing to do with the property tax relief programs that people sometimes call by a similar name.

Each householder may pick real and personal property to hold exempt, including money and debts owed to them. Part of the amount can go toward anything. A second layer applies only to property used as the principal residence of the householder or the householder's dependents.

Part of the exemptionAmount
General exemption, any property you pick$5,000
General exemption if the householder is 65 or older$10,000
Principal residence of the householder or dependentsUp to $50,000 in value
Each dependent, when support is shownUp to $500
Veteran with a service-connected disability rated 40 percent or more (34-4.1)Additional $10,000

A dependent is a person who receives most of their support from the householder and lacks the assets to support themselves. Nobody can be a dependent of more than one householder.

Inflation adjustments

The limits will move. An inflation adjustment is scheduled for April 1, 2027 and every three years after that, based on the change in the CPI-U over the latest three-year period and rounded to the nearest $25.

Bankruptcy cases begun before April 1, 2027 are not subject to the adjustment. Since your numbers depend on the filing date, confirm the current figures with the circuit court clerk or a debtor-creditor attorney before you rely on any summary.

Claiming the exemption on real estate

For real estate, you sign a homestead deed, have it acknowledged, and record it the way you would record any deed. The procedure is in Va. Code 34-6. Nothing makes it happen automatically.

  • Record the deed in the county or city where the real estate sits. For property outside Virginia, record it where the householder lives in the Commonwealth.
  • The deed must declare your intent to claim the exemption and describe the property with reasonable certainty, along with your cash valuation.
  • The statute supplies a form asking for the householder's name, the names and ages of dependents, whether the veteran add-on is claimed, and any earlier homestead deeds.
  • In a federal bankruptcy case, the filed schedule of property claimed as exempt is enough to set the property apart.

Personal property follows the same path under 34-14, except the writing is recorded where the householder lives. You can set the exemption apart at any time before the property is sold under creditor process or by a bankruptcy trustee. If wages are being garnished, the claim can be filed once the summons has been served on the employer, up to and including the return date.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Virginia house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Debts that can defeat a claim

Section 34-5 bars the exemption against two things: the purchase price of the property, and spousal or child support. A waiver can also override it. Under 34-22, someone who writes a waiver on a bond, note, or other instrument can have exempt property reached for that debt.

The wording is brief: a statement that the signer waives the benefit of the exemption as to that obligation. In practice a lender may already have asked you to give up the protection when you borrowed.

A mortgage, deed of trust, or other lien can be enforced against the property first, without the creditor exhausting other assets. The homestead gives way to that sort of secured claim because the real estate was set apart subject to paramount encumbrances.

Selling a homestead property

You can sell a homestead like any other real estate, and the buyer does not have to check how you spend the money. Section 34-9 says exempt real estate may be sold, conveyed, or exchanged, and the purchaser is not bound to see to the application of the purchase money.

  • Proceeds you reinvest are exempt in the new property to the same extent as in the old (34-20).
  • Property bought in an exchange or without a court order needs its own recorded writing stating where the funds came from.
  • Rents and profits from exempt property are exempt the same way (34-18).
  • The right to claim ends if you stop being a householder or leave Virginia (34-24).
  • Amounts you set apart count against your maximum for eight years (34-21).

Section 34-13 adds that the residence part of the exemption can be used only on that kind of property and its proceeds, not on other assets. A creditor may also ask a court to reach any value above the limit if the property was worth more than the exemption when you set it apart (34-19).

Homestead exemption versus property tax relief

Property tax relief cuts or defers the local real estate tax bill, and its rules come from a different part of the Code. The two most common programs are local and veteran based.

  • Under 58.1-3210, a locality may by ordinance exempt or defer real estate tax on the sole dwelling of an owner who is at least 65 or, if the ordinance says so, permanently and totally disabled.
  • The ordinance may limit the break to the increase in tax since the year the owner turned 65 or became disabled, or since the ordinance began, whichever is later.
  • Under 58.1-3219.5, a veteran rated 100 percent service-connected and permanently and totally disabled is exempt on a principal residence plus up to one acre, for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2011.
  • A surviving spouse keeps that exemption until remarriage and can move to a new residence without losing it.

The elderly and disabled program is a local choice, so your city or county sets the age, income, and net worth rules. Call the local Commissioner of the Revenue or Treasurer to ask what applies.

Does it matter if you want to sell fast?

It can, when an owner is behind on bills and judgment creditors might go after the house. A homestead deed protects a fixed amount of value. Anything above that can still be pursued, so the sale price and the liens on the title often matter more than the exemption alone.

Before closing, an attorney who handles debtor-creditor work in Virginia can tell you whether recording a homestead deed is worth the trouble. If you are weighing a quick sale, we can talk through your situation, and a title search will show what liens a closing has to clear.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Virginia homestead exemption?

A householder can protect $5,000 of chosen property ($10,000 at 65 or older), up to $50,000 of value in a principal residence, and up to $500 per dependent under 34-4. Inflation adjustments begin April 1, 2027.

Do I have to file a homestead deed?

For real estate, yes. Sign a writing, have it acknowledged, and record it in the county or city where the property sits. In bankruptcy, the filed schedule of exemptions can serve as the setting-apart document.

Does it protect against child support or a purchase money loan?

No. Section 34-5 bars the exemption against the purchase price of the property and against spousal or child support.

Can I sell a house I set apart as a homestead?

Yes. The buyer does not have to watch how you use the money. Proceeds you reinvest stay exempt to the same extent if the new property is documented properly.

Is this the same as the senior property tax break?

No. The homestead exemption shields property from creditors. The senior and disabled tax relief in 58.1-3210 is a local program that lowers or defers real estate tax, and each locality sets its own terms.

Does Virginia have an estate or inheritance tax?

No. The state dropped both its estate tax and its inheritance tax. Receiving a house from a relative creates no Virginia death tax bill.

You may still hear otherwise because the rules changed. Until July 1, 2007, Virginia's estate tax was tied to the federal credit for state death taxes. Once Washington eliminated that credit, the Virginia tax went with it.

One narrow exception remains: certain remainder interests are still subject to the inheritance tax. Public Document 15-93 has a section on them. When the house moves through a life estate or a trust remainder, check with a probate attorney or the Department of Taxation first instead of assuming zero.

Quick reference

ChargeAmountWho it hits
Estate taxNone today; repealed in effect after July 1, 2007Heirs of any house
Inheritance taxNone, except certain remainder interestsHeirs of life estates or trust remainders
Probate tax10 cents per $100 of estate valueEstates over $15,000
Deed grantor tax50 cents per $500 of considerationWhoever signs the sale deed

Only two of these charges apply to a normal estate sale: the probate tax when the estate opens, and the deed tax when the house sells. Both are explained below.

Virginia probate tax

The probate tax is charged when a will is probated or an administrator is appointed, and it follows the size of the estate, not the identity of the heirs.

Code 58.1-1712 sets the rate at 10 cents per $100 of value, with any leftover fraction of $100 counted. Estates of $15,000 or less are exempt. Section 58.1-1713, the next one, governs how value is determined.

For current steps and any filing fees, ask the circuit court clerk in the city or county where the person lived.

Order of events for an estate sale

The order is usually the same. First the will goes to probate at the circuit court. The named executor qualifies, or the court appoints an administrator when there is no will or no executor, and the probate tax comes due at that point. With the certificate of qualification in hand, the personal representative can list the house or take a cash offer.

Then the title company searches title, requests a payoff from the Treasurer, and confirms the signer's authority. Ask the title officer early for a written list of anything the clerk's office must still supply. Closing day brings the recorded deed and the grantor tax, paid through the clerk. Property tax and any mortgage come out of the proceeds, and the remainder belongs to the estate. A cash buyer shortens the middle stretch, since no lender underwriting or appraisal holds things up.

Heirs in other states can generally leave the signing to the personal representative.

Who has authority to sell

Under Code 64.2-521, an executor may sell and convey real estate and collect the proceeds when the will directs a sale and leaves the job to no one else.

If no executor qualifies, or the ones who did die, resign, or are removed, an administrator with the will annexed holds that power too, unless the will clearly says otherwise.

Before listing, collect:

  • The will, plus the certificate naming the personal representative.
  • Any direction in the will to sell the real estate.
  • The deed, the newest tax bill, and the latest mortgage statement.
  • The title company's list of papers it needs from the clerk's office.

No state estate tax payment appears on that list. The title company can say which authority papers it wants.

Property tax still attached to the house

A death does not clear the property tax. It stays with the house and ranks first: Code 58.1-3340 puts the real estate tax lien ahead of every other lien or encumbrance until the taxing authority has been paid.

Penalties and interest count as taxes under that section, and sale proceeds must cover taxes and levies on the real estate first. The purchase agreement prorates the seller's share, so it should spell out who pays for which dates.

Localities set their own schedules, and Virginia Beach is one example. Its bills come due in two installments, December 5 and June 5. A late payment costs a 10% penalty or $10, whichever is greater, plus 9.6% yearly interest. Unpaid taxes can lead the city to record a lien at the Circuit Court clerk, and once delinquency reaches three years plus the current tax year the Treasurer can advertise the property and charge a $25 fee.

Inherited a house with back taxes? Get a payoff figure from the local Treasurer before you list. Closing pays it out of the proceeds.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Virginia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Deed tax when heirs sell

The estate owes the grantor tax on the deed, as any seller would. Code 58.1-802 charges 50 cents per $500 of consideration, rounding up any fraction. The grantor pays it unless the contract shifts part or all of it to the buyer.

Recording requires the consideration on the deed's first page and the clerk's certification that the tax was paid. The clerk collects the money and divides it between the state and the locality.

Whether the estate or the buyer bears it follows the contract.

Federal tax on an inherited sale

No state death tax does not make the sale tax free, because the IRS can still tax a gain. An inherited house gets its basis under special rules in Publication 551, Basis of Assets, rather than from what the decedent paid. Publication 544 covers the holding-period exceptions for property from a decedent. Whether there is any gain turns on that basis and the final sale price.

  • Find out from the estate's preparer how basis was set.
  • The $250,000 and $500,000 home sale exclusion only helps if you owned the home and lived in it as your main residence for 24 of the last 5 years.
  • A Form 1099-S means the sale must be reported, even if the gain is excluded.
  • A loss on a home used personally cannot be deducted.

A separate page on this site explains how the federal rules interact with Virginia income tax on a house sale.

When an as-is cash sale helps an estate

Families wanting a certain closing date and no repair list often prefer it, particularly while holding costs mount. Taxes, insurance, utilities, and lawn care continue until closing, and a vacant house brings added risk.

Selling as-is ends the repair haggling, which helps when the heirs are scattered across states. A title company still handles closing, and the personal representative must still show authority to convey.

Questions about paperwork or timing are welcome. We do not give tax or legal advice, so let a probate attorney confirm who may sign.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is there Virginia inheritance tax on a house I inherit?

No, with one narrow exception for certain remainder interests. A house that arrived through a life estate or trust remainder is worth a call to a probate attorney.

How much is the Virginia probate tax?

Code 58.1-1712 sets it at 10 cents per $100 of estate value. Estates of $15,000 or less owe nothing.

Does an executor need every heir to sign a sale?

Where the will directs a sale and names nobody else to handle it, Code 64.2-521 lets the executor sell and convey alone. Other wills vary, so an attorney should confirm.

Who covers unpaid property tax on an inherited house?

Closing pays it from the sale proceeds. Code 58.1-3340 ranks the tax lien first, and the contract prorates the seller's share.

Will I owe federal tax if I sell inherited property?

Maybe. Gain is taxable, and Publication 551 sets the basis rules for inherited homes. Many sales show little or no gain, but a tax professional should check.

How an eviction case starts

Every Virginia eviction begins with a request to a magistrate, a court clerk, or a general district court judge for a summons. A sworn statement of the facts that justify removing the tenant goes with it. The case is called an unlawful detainer and is filed under Va. Code 8.01-126.

In a residential case the first hearing is meant to come as soon as practicable, and no later than 21 days after filing. When the docket cannot take it that fast, it still has to be heard within 30 days. The tenant must be served at least 10 days ahead of the return date. A landlord may request a later first date, and the court then picks one that suits both sides and the court.

Paperwork sets a floor. No order of possession can be entered unless the landlord has shown the tenant a proper termination notice and the court has accepted that notice into evidence. With no notice in the record, the judge has nothing to base possession on.

Owners thinking of selling a rented house should know that court calendars and notice periods decide how long the tenant stays, not the day you choose to list.

Notice periods before filing

What the tenant did decides which notice applies, and each has its own clock under Va. Code 55.1-1245. These are the pieces that matter most when a rented house is headed for sale.

SituationWhat the landlord must do
Unpaid rentGive written notice, then wait 14 days for the tenant to pay before terminating and suing for possession
Breach that can be fixedGive notice that the lease ends no sooner than 30 days after receipt unless the problem is fixed within 21 days
Breach that cannot be fixedGive notice that the lease ends no sooner than 30 days after receipt
Criminal or willful act threatening health or safetyEnd the lease immediately and seek possession; first hearing within 15 calendar days of service
Repeat breach of the same kindGive a 30-day notice that refers to the earlier breach
Tenant who is a family abuse victimLease does not end solely because of abuse against the tenant, if the abuser is barred by the landlord or a court order

A fixable breach does not end the lease when the tenant fixes it before the date in the notice. On a rent default, that window is how a tenant who catches up keeps the home.

Landlords with more than four rentals

From July 1, 2027, a landlord with more than four rental units, or more than a 10 percent interest in more than four, must offer a payment plan before using the 14-day pay-or-quit route in certain small-balance cases. The Virginia legislature's text of 55.1-1245 shows the version for that date next to the current one.

  • It applies when the exact rent owed is no more than one month's rent plus contracted late charges.
  • The notice states the exact amount and offers equal monthly installments over the shorter of six months or the time left on the lease.
  • The tenant may pay off the balance early without penalty, and no extra late fees accrue while payments are on time.
  • The landlord has to make the offer only once during the rental agreement.
  • A tenant who neither pays nor enters the plan within 14 days can be terminated, and the landlord proceeds to court.

Owners of four or fewer units fall outside that subsection. With a single rented house you will usually serve the ordinary 14-day notice, but read your lease and ask a Virginia attorney which version applies on the day you serve it.

After the judge awards possession

With a possession judgment in hand, the landlord requests a writ of eviction and the sheriff carries it out. Timing comes from two statutes, 8.01-129 and 8.01-471.

  • The tenant has 10 days from judgment to appeal to circuit court. The appeal bond and writ tax are due within those 10 days.
  • A defendant found indigent is excused from the appeal bond.
  • On request, the judge can order the writ to issue at once, but the sheriff cannot evict until the 10-day appeal period is over.
  • The sheriff serves notice of the eviction date and time at least 72 hours before executing the writ.
  • If the tenant perfects an appeal, the sheriff returns the writ to the clerk who issued it.

Issuance has to happen within 180 days of the judgment. After that the writ is returnable within 30 days, and one that goes unexecuted for that long is vacated by operation of law without another order. No writ can issue if landlord and tenant sign a new written rental agreement after the judgment.

What a landlord can collect besides possession

Under Va. Code 55.1-1251, ending the lease gives the landlord a claim for possession and rent. A separate claim covers actual damages, reasonable attorney fees, and the cost of serving notices and process.

Actual damages may include rent that would have fallen due until the term ends or a new tenancy starts, whichever comes first. The landlord must work to limit them, and a post-possession damages case cannot seek accelerated rent through the end of the term.

The court can award possession and a money judgment together, and the money judgment need not be reduced by the security deposit first. Once the tenant is gone, whether by choice or by writ, the deposit is credited under the deposit statute, which allows 45 days for an itemized statement.

These claims belong to the landlord. Whether a particular judgment stays with the seller or moves with the house depends on the contract, so have an attorney read it before closing.

Selling a rented house with an eviction pending

An open eviction does not block a sale. It does change what the buyer takes on. The closing transfers a deed, and the tenant's rights survive a change of owner.

  • Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the security deposit statute and must return any deposit owed, even if it never changed hands with the property.
  • No unlawful detainer for a lease violation can be filed or kept going until the tenant has received the statement of tenant rights and responsibilities.
  • A hearing date, an appeal, or an unexecuted writ can push back the day the house is empty, so leave room in the closing date.

Cash Home Buyers talks with owners in every one of these positions, including houses with tenants in place. A conversation about the lease and any court papers is the quickest way to see what a sale would involve. We do not give legal advice, so take the eviction file to an attorney too.

Former owners after a foreclosure sale

A former owner still living in a single-family home on the day of the foreclosure sale is treated by Virginia as a tenant at sufferance. The new owner can end that tenancy by written notice given at least three days before the termination date, then file an unlawful detainer once the three days run out.

Fair rental value is owed from the foreclosure date until the person leaves, along with damages and reasonable attorney fees and court costs. The rule sits in 8.01-126, the same section that governs the eviction case.

Someone who rented from the foreclosed owner is a different case with different notice rules, described earlier on this page. If you cannot tell which category an occupant is in, ask the clerk of your local general district court before filing.

Local court details

Each general district court keeps its own docket, filing hours, and fee schedule, and some localities attach local resource sheets to the summons. Call the clerk of the court where the rental house sits for current filing steps, fees, and hearing days.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Virginia eviction take from notice to lockout?

No single number fits. A 14-day rent notice, a first hearing 21 to 30 days after filing, a 10-day appeal window, and at least 72 hours of sheriff notice each add time, and an appeal adds more.

Can a landlord remove a tenant without a court order?

No. Only a sheriff executing a writ of eviction can remove a tenant, and the writ follows a possession judgment in an unlawful detainer case.

How long is a writ of eviction valid?

It must issue within 180 days of the judgment and is returnable within 30 days of issuance. If it is not executed in 30 days it is vacated automatically.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying?

Often, if done before the notice period ends. A rent notice allows 14 days to pay, and a fixable breach does not end the lease if fixed in time. After judgment, a new written rental agreement blocks the writ.

Who keeps the security deposit if the rental is sold?

Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends must return any deposit owed to the tenant, even if the deposit did not change hands at closing.

What a transfer on death deed is

Think of it as a recorded deed that names the person who receives a Virginia property at the owner's death, with no trip through the owner's will. Under Article 5 of Title 64.2, an individual may transfer property to one or more beneficiaries effective at the transferor's death. The statute calls the owner the transferor and the person named to receive the property the designated beneficiary.

The law reaches an interest in real property in the Commonwealth. Deeds made before, on, or after July 1, 2013 are covered, provided the transferor died on or after that date. Nothing here replaces the other options: a will, a trust, or joint ownership still work.

Lawyers call the deed nontestamentary. It is a deed whose effect is delayed until death, so it follows the formalities of a deed and not the signing rules of a will.

What the deed must contain to be valid

Seven requirements appear in Va. Code 64.2-628, and a deed that misses even one can fail. Check each against your own paperwork.

  • The deed has to carry everything a normal recordable lifetime deed would.
  • Its wording must say the beneficiary receives the property when the transferor dies.
  • Recording has to happen while the transferor is alive, in the circuit court clerk's land records where the property sits.
  • Chapter 6 of Title 55.1 sets the recording rules, and the clerk indexes the deed with the transferor as grantor.
  • With no consideration involved, recordation tax does not apply.
  • Property with joint owners needs every joint owner's signature.
  • For the purposes of Va. Code 17.1-223, it is treated as a deed.

The mental capacity needed to sign or revoke is the capacity needed to make a will. Nobody has to tell the beneficiary, the beneficiary does not have to accept, and no payment is needed.

Changing or canceling the deed

Owners can change their minds. Va. Code 64.2-625 makes the deed revocable even when the deed or another document says otherwise, and the owner stays fully in control for life.

Revoking takes a recorded document, and the law names four kinds in section 64.2-630:

  • A later transfer on death deed that expressly revokes the first, fully or partly.
  • A later transfer on death deed naming a beneficiary that conflicts with the first.
  • A stand-alone instrument of revocation stating that purpose expressly.
  • An ordinary deed to someone else, which leaves nothing owned at death.

Any revoking document must be acknowledged after the original deed was, and recorded before the owner dies in the same circuit court land records. Once a deed is recorded, destroying or marking up your copy accomplishes nothing. When several owners signed, one owner's revocation does not undo the others' share, and a deed made by joint owners is revoked only if every living joint owner revokes it. An optional revocation form appears at 64.2-636.

What happens at the owner's death

Under Va. Code 64.2-632, ownership vests in the designated beneficiary only if that person is alive when the owner dies. A beneficiary who dies first gets nothing.

Details matter when a deed names several people or a family changes over time.

  • Several beneficiaries split the property into equal undivided shares, and none has survivorship rights.
  • When one of them fails or lapses, the others absorb that share in proportion to their own.
  • A later divorce or annulment cancels a gift to the former spouse, unless the deed provides differently.
  • A surviving co-owner takes the property if the transferor was a joint owner, though still subject to the named beneficiary.

What the beneficiary gets is the property as it stood at death, burdened by every conveyance, mortgage, lien, and other interest. No covenant or warranty of title comes with it, whatever the deed says. Chapter 26 of Title 64.2 lets a beneficiary turn down some or all of the interest.

Creditors and the owner's lifetime

While the owner is alive, the deed changes nothing and protects the property from nobody. Section 64.2-631 spells out what it leaves alone.

  • The owner can still sell, mortgage, or otherwise deal with the property.
  • Creditors, present or future, keep every right they had, whether or not they know about the deed.
  • Public assistance eligibility stays the same for both the owner and the beneficiary.
  • The beneficiary holds no legal or equitable interest yet.
  • The property is not open to claims against the beneficiary.

Death changes things. Under section 64.2-634, property that passed by deed can be reached for creditors' claims, administration costs, funeral expenses, and family allowances, but only when the probate estate cannot cover them. If several properties passed by deed, each carries a share in proportion to its net value. Any proceeding to enforce this has to start within one year after the death.

Recordation tax

No recordation tax is due on recording the deed, or a revocation, when nothing is paid between the parties. The exemption sits in Va. Code 58.1-811(J), and the optional statutory forms repeat the notice at the top.

That section also covers other no-payment filings that families run into.

Selling an inherited house held through the deed

With the deed in place, a beneficiary can hold title right after the death and does not have to wait for a court to open an estate for this one house. Debts stay with the house, though, and the beneficiary inherits it as is.

For a Virginia seller that works out like this:

  • Expect to hand over the recorded deed and a death record when the buyer's side wants proof you own the house.
  • Any mortgage or lien on the house is still there at closing, since the beneficiary took it subject to those.
  • Because no title warranty comes with the transfer, the title company will study the record history closely.
  • Possible estate claims under 64.2-634 may need an answer before the title company will close.

Cash Home Buyers deals with beneficiaries who want to sell an inherited Virginia house as is, even one that needs repairs, has tenants, or owes taxes. Call us if a transfer on death deed put you on title, and we will walk through how an offer works. Title questions belong with a Virginia attorney first.

When this deed is the wrong tool

This is the wrong choice for anyone who needs a certain, permanent transfer. The owner can always revoke, and the beneficiary has no claim during the owner's life. It is also a poor fit when the owner worries the named person might die first, since a beneficiary who does not survive the owner loses the interest.

Other points to weigh with an attorney:

  • A deed recorded after the owner's death does nothing, so timing matters.
  • A deed signed by one co-owner does not bind the others, and a joint owner's deed needs every joint owner's signature to be effective.
  • Where a will leaves real estate to be sold and names no other person, the executor has the power to sell and convey under Va. Code 64.2-521, a different route from a transfer on death deed.

Frequently asked questions

Is a transfer on death deed the same as a will?

No. It is nontestamentary: a recorded deed that takes effect at death. A will is a separate document that goes through probate. Signing either one takes the same capacity.

Does the beneficiary have to sign or accept the deed?

No. The deed is effective without notice to, delivery to, or acceptance by the beneficiary during the owner's life, and without consideration.

When must the deed be recorded?

Before the owner dies. It goes in the land records of the circuit court clerk's office in the county or city where the property sits, and the clerk indexes it under the owner's name as grantor.

Can I sell my house after recording the deed?

Yes. During your life the deed does not affect your right to transfer or mortgage the property. Selling by a regular deed also revokes the earlier transfer on death deed, since you no longer own the property at death.

What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

The beneficiary's interest lapses, because it depends on surviving the owner. When several beneficiaries share the property, the lapsed share goes to the others in proportion to their interests.

Where a Virginia probate case starts

A will is offered for probate in the circuit court of the county or independent city where the person who died had a known residence. With no known residence, the next choices are a county or city where the person owned or devised real estate, then the place of death or wherever the person had other estate (Va. Code 64.2-443).

Virginia has 95 counties and 38 independent cities, and each has its own circuit court clerk. A stay in a nursing home does not move the starting point, since legal residence is presumed to stay what it was before the person became a patient.

The clerk, or a qualified deputy clerk, can admit a will to probate, appoint and qualify executors and administrators, and take their bonds, with the same effect as the court itself (Va. Code 64.2-444). Anyone interested in the probate can appeal a clerk's order to the circuit court within six months without posting a bond, and the court then hears the matter fresh (Va. Code 64.2-445).

Who can act for the estate

With a will, the named executor acts. If the will names no executor, or the executor refuses, fails to give bond, dies, resigns, or is removed, the court or clerk may grant administration with the will annexed. A residual or substantial legatee, or that person's designee, goes first. If that person does not apply within 30 days, administration can go to someone who would have been entitled to it had there been no will (Va. Code 64.2-500).

Without a will, Va. Code 64.2-502 spells out who may apply and when:

  • First 30 days: a sole distributee, or one distributee holding written waivers from all other competent distributees.
  • After 30 days: the first distributee, or designee, who applies. If several gave notice of intent during the first 30 days, there is a hearing.
  • After 45 days: a nonprofit charitable organization that was conservator or guardian, following a diligent search and certified mail notice.
  • After 60 days: a creditor or other person, following a diligent search for distributees and certified mail notice at least 30 days before applying.

The clerk must be satisfied that the applicant is suitable and competent. The applicant swears that he or she is not under a legal disability and has not been convicted of certain felonies involving fraud, theft, or similar offenses. An exception applies when the convicted person is the sole distributee.

The small asset affidavit and a house

The small asset affidavit lets successors collect certain assets without opening a full estate, but it reaches personal property, not a deed to real estate. It works only when the whole personal probate estate is $75,000 or less (Va. Code 64.2-601).

All known successors make the affidavit on a form prepared by the Office of the Executive Secretary of the Supreme Court of Virginia. It must state:

  • that the personal probate estate does not exceed $75,000;
  • that at least 60 days have gone by since the death;
  • that no application for a personal representative is pending or granted anywhere;
  • that any will was duly probated;
  • who the successors are and who is designated to receive the asset, with a fiduciary duty to safeguard and deliver it.

A house is real estate, so heirs who want to sell usually need a personal representative or a will that gives someone the power to sell. If you are unsure which route fits your family, the circuit court clerk can explain the paperwork the court accepts.

Can an executor sell the house?

Yes, when the will directs that the real estate be sold and names nobody else to handle the sale. The executor then has the power to sell and convey the property and to receive the proceeds (Va. Code 64.2-521).

If no executor qualifies, or the ones who did have died, resigned, or been removed, an administrator with the will annexed holds that power unless the will clearly says otherwise. Where the will is silent about a sale, or there is no will, the heirs often sign the deed together. A title company will want the court's grant of authority and the names of every heir.

Deadlines and costs

Within four months after the order giving authority, the personal representative files an inventory with the commissioner of accounts. It lists the personal estate and all real estate over which the representative has the power of sale, with a market value for each item as of the date of death (Va. Code 64.2-1300). Reasonable expenses of finding those values count as costs of administration.

A probate tax applies to every will probated and every grant of administration, at 10 cents for each $100 of estate value. Estates of $15,000 or less are exempt (Va. Code 58.1-1712).

Who gets paid first

When assets cannot cover every claim, Virginia pays in a set order, and administration costs come first. Next come the family allowances, funeral expenses up to $5,000, and debts and taxes with preference under federal law. After those are medical and hospital bills of the last illness, capped at $4,000 per hospital or nursing home and $550 per person providing services or goods. Then come debts and taxes due the Commonwealth, certain fiduciary debts, child support arrears, and debts and taxes due localities. All other claims share what is left (Va. Code 64.2-528).

A mortgage on an inherited house

As a rule the mortgage stays with the property. Unless the will, a revocable trust, or a transfer on death deed clearly says otherwise, specifically devised real property passes subject to any lien in place at death, and the heir cannot make the estate pay it off first. A general instruction in the will to pay debts does not change that (Va. Code 64.2-531).

The personal representative may send the lender written notice by certified mail. The creditor then has until the later of one year after qualification or six months after the notice to file a claim with the commissioner of accounts. The statute also gives the representative a path to sell specifically devised property subject to a claim if the estate is not released within the time it sets.

Transfer taxes on the sale

A deed admitted to record carries a state recordation tax of 25 cents on every $100 of the greater of the deed's consideration or the property's most recent tax assessment (Va. Code 58.1-801). A separate grantor tax of 50 cents per $500 applies to a deed for realty that was sold. The seller pays it unless buyer and seller arrange otherwise (Va. Code 58.1-802).

The consideration goes on the first page of the deed, and the clerk certifies payment before recording. Local recordation taxes may also apply, so ask the circuit court clerk for the current total in the county or city where the house stands.

Unpaid property tax on an estate house

Real estate taxes are a lien that ranks ahead of other liens until paid, and the buyer or trustee at a sale must see that proceeds go to the taxes due (Va. Code 58.1-3340). The estate should expect any back taxes to be settled at closing.

Local governing bodies set due dates, penalties, and interest by ordinance. When a payment is late because of the taxpayer's death or a medically determinable impairment, the lateness is presumed not to be the taxpayer's fault if paid within 30 days of the due date, or within 120 days after a fiduciary qualifies. Interest keeps running either way (Va. Code 58.1-3916).

In practice, collect the payoff letters from the Treasurer and the lender before listing, so the title company and the buyer see the same numbers. A cash sale can close as soon as authority and title are in order, without waiting on a buyer's loan.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Do I need probate to sell a house in Virginia?

Usually yes. When the house is titled only in the decedent's name, a personal representative or a will with power of sale is generally needed before a title company will insure the sale. A small asset affidavit covers personal property up to $75,000, not a deed.

How long do I have to inventory the estate?

Four months after the order giving the personal representative authority. The inventory goes to the commissioner of accounts and lists real estate over which the representative holds the power of sale.

Can a creditor be appointed to run an estate?

Yes, but only after 60 days from the death, and only after a diligent search for distributees and certified mail notice sent at least 30 days before the application.

Is there a Virginia probate tax?

Yes, 10 cents for each $100 of estate value. Estates of $15,000 or less are exempt.

Does a mortgage have to be paid off before heirs inherit?

Generally no. A specifically devised house passes subject to its mortgage unless the will or trust clearly directs payoff. The lender can still file a claim with the commissioner of accounts within the statutory time.

Federal exclusion eligibility

Qualifying takes 24 months of ownership and 24 months of living there as your primary home, both measured inside the five years that end on the closing date. Those months can come from different periods and don't need to be consecutive.

On a joint return one spouse can supply the ownership months, but each spouse must separately have the living months. Using the exclusion on a different house during the previous two years usually shuts it off.

  • Ownership months: 24 within the last 5 years.
  • Primary-residence months: 24 within the last 5 years.
  • No exclusion claimed on another sale in the past two years.
  • Extended-duty members of the military, Foreign Service or intelligence community can suspend the five-year count for up to 10 years.

For worksheets and exceptions, see IRS Publication 523, Selling Your Home.

Rental and investment houses

Rentals and investment houses usually can't use the home sale exclusion, which leaves a taxable capital gain. If you held the property over a year the gain is long-term; at a year or less it is short-term and taxed at ordinary income rates.

For 2025 the long-term federal rate has three steps. It is 0% on taxable income up to $48,350 for single filers and $96,700 for joint filers, 15% from there to $533,400 single or $600,050 joint, and 20% beyond.

Landlords should know two more federal items. The slice of gain that comes from depreciation, called unrecaptured section 1250 gain, tops out at a 25% rate. Higher-income sellers may also face the net investment income tax (IRS Topic 559).

These federal rates stack on top of the Virginia rates above, because Virginia taxes the gain as income.

Working out your gain

The formula is simple: amount realized minus adjusted basis. Your basis begins at the purchase price plus buying costs, rises for value-adding improvements, and falls for depreciation and casualty insurance payouts.

Hang on to receipts for roofs, additions and remodels, since each raises basis and cuts the taxable gain. If you sell your own home at a loss, there is no deduction.

  • Start from the contract price and settlement statement.
  • Raise your cost by documented capital improvements.
  • Lower it by depreciation if any part was rented out.
  • Compare what remains with the $250,000 or $500,000 cap.

Gifts and inheritances follow their own basis rules, spelled out in IRS Publication 551, Basis of Assets. Look there before you pick a number.

Order of work for a Virginia seller

If you are about to sell and want to know what tax to expect, work through it in this order.

  1. Label the property as your main home, a rental or an inheritance, because that label drives everything after it.
  2. If it is your main home, tally the months you owned and lived in it. Hitting 24 within the last 5 years generally settles the federal exclusion.
  3. Collect your purchase paperwork and the receipts for roofs, additions and remodels to build your basis.
  4. Confirm you haven't used the exclusion on another sale recently.
  5. Get the settlement statement from the closing agent, and expect a Form 1099-S later.
  6. Apply Virginia's brackets to any gain left over and set cash aside in case estimated payments are needed.

A tax professional can check each step. This list only shows what to ask.

Paperwork after closing

Receiving a Form 1099-S, Proceeds From Real Estate Transactions, puts the sale on your return even when the entire gain is excludable. A partly taxable gain gets reported too, using Form 8949 and Schedule D where they apply.

When the buyer pays part of the price in a later year, the installment method applies unless you elect out. Spreading gain over time this way leaves the home sale exclusion intact.

IRS Publication 505 explains the estimated payments a large gain can trigger.

Other Virginia costs at closing

Two non-income-tax items shrink a Virginia seller's proceeds: the state grantor tax on the deed and any real estate tax still owed.

Code 58.1-802 sets the grantor tax at 50 cents on every $500 of consideration. The seller owes it unless the parties agree to another split. A clerk of court certifies it before the deed is recorded, and the state and locality each keep half.

Under Code 58.1-3340 the lien for real estate tax outranks all other liens. Sale proceeds go first to taxes and levies on the property, and your contract prorates your portion of the year's tax.

Billing calendars vary by locality. Virginia Beach collects on December 5 and June 5.

Inherited houses and depreciation

Inherited property isn't valued at what the decedent paid. Publication 551 explains how basis works for it, and Publication 544 handles holding periods for property from a decedent.

On a rental, claimed depreciation lowers basis and can create the section 1250 gain mentioned above. A tenant in the house raises lease questions too, and the Virginia eviction notice guide on this site covers them.

  • Inherited: confirm basis before you price the house.
  • Rental: add up depreciation across all your years of ownership.
  • Primary home: test the 24-month rules before an offer arrives.

Tax angle on a fast as-is sale

It can pay off when carrying costs, repairs or an approaching tax bill would cost you more than the discount. An early closing stops the monthly mortgage, insurance and property tax drain and gives you a set date for planning.

The buyer's identity doesn't alter your tax, because gain comes from price and basis. Speed changes your timing, your carrying payments and the repairs you skip.

Get a CPA or enrolled agent to run your figures before accepting anything. We buy houses as-is and can share a closing timeline, but tax advice isn't something we give.

Frequently asked questions

Does Virginia have a capital gains tax?

There's no separate tax. Gain is treated as income at Virginia's ordinary rates, topping out at 5.75% above $17,000 under Code 58.1-320.

How much gain can I exclude when I sell my Virginia home?

As much as $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you've owned and lived in the house 24 months of the past 5 years. Virginia goes along with the federal rule.

Do I report the sale if the whole gain is excluded?

If a Form 1099-S came, yes, even with a fully excludable gain. You also report it when only part of the gain is excludable.

How long must I own a rental house for long-term capital gain treatment?

Over a year. Selling at one year or sooner produces a short-term gain, taxed as ordinary income.

Who pays the Virginia grantor tax?

Normally the seller, at 50 cents per $500 of consideration. A contract can shift part or all of it to the buyer.

How a Virginia tax sale works

The locality begins by suing in the circuit court of the county or city where the property sits. The suit enforces the lien for delinquent taxes and asks the court to sell the real estate (Va. Code 58.1-3967). Procedure follows the rules for a creditor's suit to sell real estate on a judgment lien, except where a statute says something different.

Everyone with an interest has to be named: lienors, anyone claiming title, and the beneficiary and trustees under a deed of trust. Title passes at the judicial sale free of those parties' claims, and former owners can claim surplus afterward.

When a property can be sold for delinquent taxes

The usual trigger is tax still delinquent on December 31 after the second anniversary of the date it came due. A property with a condemned structure, a nuisance, a derelict building, or a blighted declaration can be reached after the first anniversary instead (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

Real estate assessed at $100,000 or less gets different treatment. Once the court finds taxes delinquent on December 31 after the first anniversary, the property is deemed subject to sale at public auction after proper notice. Certain unpaid local lien costs for abatement or repair work the same way.

SituationEarliest sale trigger
Ordinary parcelDecember 31 after the second anniversary of the due date
Condemned, nuisance, derelict, or blightedDecember 31 after the first anniversary
Assessed at $100,000 or less (court finding)December 31 after the first anniversary

In a qualifying locality with unpaid abatement costs, the periods for the condemned and blighted categories can shrink to six months.

Notice to the owner

At least 30 days before starting court action, the collecting officer must send notice to the owner's last known address in the treasurer's records. If the property address differs and is a numbered, named street address, the notice goes there too. It tells the owner that a payment agreement of up to 72 months may be requested (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

The officer also publishes a list of the properties at least once in a local newspaper, again at least 30 days before the case is filed. Publication costs, the court's reasonable attorney fees, and title examination costs are added to what the owner owes, even when the owner pays before any case is filed.

If you move often or live out of state, keep the treasurer's records current. A notice mailed to an old address helps no one. An owner served only by publication may petition for a rehearing, but only for good cause and only within 90 days after the sale is confirmed.

How an owner can stop the sale

Pay everything owed before the sale date. An owner may redeem at any time up to the sale by paying the accumulated taxes, penalties, interest, reasonable attorney fees, and costs, including the pro rata cost of publication. Paying part of the balance does not redeem the property or stop the lawsuit (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

Heirs, devisees, successors, and assigns have the same right and redeem by paying into court before the sale date. Whoever pays taxes on the property gets a lien for the amount paid, with interest at six percent a year (Va. Code 58.1-3974).

The statute offers other options too:

  • The treasurer may suspend the sale under an installment agreement of up to 72 months, which must also cover current taxes as they come due.
  • A person who is not a party but claims ownership through a will or intestate succession can send written notice to the treasurer, who may suspend the case and ask the court to add that person as a party.
  • The court may refer the parties to a dispute resolution proceeding.

Miss a payment on an installment plan and the treasurer can void it on 15 days' written notice. The case then goes forward without repeating the notice, and no second plan is available for three years.

Heirs when the owner has died

Heirs have a path built in. A person who claims ownership by will or by intestate succession can notify the treasurer in writing, and the treasurer may suspend the action while seeking leave to add that person as a party. If the court finds the person holds an ownership interest, that person has 30 days to enter an installment agreement for the delinquent amounts, over no more than 72 months (Va. Code 58.1-3965).

An estate problem and a tax problem meet here. If probate has not started, the person with the strongest claim should contact both the circuit court clerk and the treasurer quickly. Our Virginia probate guide explains who can qualify.

The cost of waiting

Costs grow three ways. Penalty and interest keep accruing under the locality's ordinance, with interest capped at 10 percent a year at first and a higher ceiling in later years. The locality may also recover attorney or collection agency fees actually contracted for, up to 20 percent of the delinquent taxes and charges (Va. Code 58.1-3916).

The third is the lien itself. Real estate tax ranks ahead of every other lien and stays there until actual payment, so a buyer or lender cannot work around it, and any sale needs the tax paid from proceeds (Va. Code 58.1-3340). It covers rents for the current year as well.

Surplus after a judicial sale

The former owner and the heirs, devisees, successors, or assigns are entitled to what is left after taxes, penalties, interest, reasonable attorney fees, costs, and liens. The claimant carries the burden of proving entitlement. If no one claims the surplus within two years after the sale is confirmed, the clerk pays it to the locality. A governing body may grant relief by ordinance and pay a person who shows prior entitlement whatever amount it considers appropriate (Va. Code 58.1-3967).

The grantor's transfer tax of 50 cents per $500 does not apply when the grantor is a locality at a judicial sale of tax-delinquent property (Va. Code 58.1-802).

Selling before the sale date

A private sale lets you pick the buyer and the timing, and the tax lien comes out of the proceeds, so the rest is yours. A judicial sale runs on the court's schedule, and surplus can take time and proof to claim. If the case grows, costs can also eat the equity in a house with a lien.

Each locality has its own treasurer's office and circuit court, so the list, the notices, and the fees depend on where the house stands. Ask the treasurer for a written payoff, ask the circuit court clerk whether a case has been filed, and compare that payoff to what a buyer is offering. A cash purchase can close quickly enough to beat a sale date, as long as the payoff and the title are in order.

Frequently asked questions

Can I stop a tax sale by paying part of what I owe?

No. Partial payment does not redeem the property and does not suspend or end the court action. Redemption takes all taxes, penalties, interest, attorney fees, and costs, unless the treasurer agrees to an installment plan.

How long can a payment plan last?

Up to 72 months, and it must also keep current taxes paid as they come due. If you default, the treasurer can void the plan on 15 days' written notice.

Does the locality have to warn me before suing?

Yes. Notice must go out at least 30 days before court action, to the owner's address on file and to the property address if different, and a list of properties must be published in a local newspaper.

Do heirs have rights if the owner died?

Yes. Heirs, devisees, successors, and assigns may redeem before the sale, and a person claiming through a will or intestate succession can ask the treasurer to suspend the case.

Who gets the money if the property sells for more than the taxes?

The former owner and heirs, devisees, successors, or assigns, after taxes, fees, costs, and liens, if they prove entitlement within two years of confirmation. After that it goes to the locality.
